questions.title: Redis Overview and Use Cases
questions.question: What is Redis and what are its main use cases in a Java backend application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Redis: in-memory data structure store — used as cache, message broker, session store, rate limiter
- Persistence options: RDB snapshots, AOF (append-only file) — persistence is optional
- Single-threaded command execution — no race conditions on individual commands
- Sub-millisecond latency — orders of magnitude faster than disk-based databases
- Main use cases: caching (L2 cache), session storage, distributed locks, pub/sub, rate limiting, leaderboards
- Redis Cluster: horizontal scaling for large datasets
- Eviction policies: LRU, LFU, allkeys-lru for cache use

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Redis is an in-memory data structure store that operates at sub-millisecond latency — typically under a millisecond for simple operations. This makes it orders of magnitude faster than a relational database for the kinds of operations where raw speed matters: caching frequently queried data, storing user sessions, implementing distributed locks, and building real-time leaderboards.

The key architectural decision is that Redis is single-threaded for command execution. This means each command executes atomically without concurrent modification — no race conditions on individual operations. When two clients write the same key simultaneously, Redis serializes those writes in the order they arrive.

For a Java Spring Boot backend, the most common uses are as an L2 cache to reduce database load, as a session store for distributed sessions across multiple application instances, and as a shared distributed lock to coordinate actions that should only happen on one instance at a time — like a scheduled job or inventory reservation.

questions.title: Redis Strings and Hashes
questions.question: How do Redis strings and hashes work and what are practical use cases for each?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- String: most versatile type — stores text, binary, JSON, serialized objects, numbers
- SET / GET / DEL / EXISTS / EXPIRE / TTL — basic string operations
- INCR / INCRBY: atomic increment — counters, rate limiting
- SETNX (SET NX): set only if not exists — basis of distributed locks
- Hash: map of field-value pairs — like a row in a table or a Java Map
- HSET / HGET / HMSET / HGETALL / HDEL — hash operations
- Hash vs JSON string: hash allows field-level operations without deserializing everything

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Redis strings are the simplest and most versatile data type. Despite the name, they can hold any binary data up to 512MB — text, serialized objects, JSON, even binary files. For caching a database query result, you serialize the result to JSON and store it as a string with a TTL. When the cache entry expires, the next request goes to the database and repopulates it.

The INCR command is where strings become powerful for counters. It atomically reads a number, increments it, and writes it back — all in one operation. This is exactly what you need for rate limiting: INCR user:123:requests:2024010114 (user ID + hour bucket), then check if the value exceeds your limit. If the key doesn't exist, Redis creates it with value 0 and returns 1.

Hashes are a natural fit for object storage when you need field-level access. A user session stored as a hash lets you update individual fields — like the last activity timestamp — without reading and rewriting the entire session object. This is more efficient than storing the whole session as a JSON string when you only need to update one field.

speakable_v2.hook: Redis strings are the simplest and most versatile data type.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This is more efficient than storing the whole session as a JSON string when you only need to update one field.

questions.title: Redis Lists, Sets and Sorted Sets
questions.question: How do Redis Lists, Sets, and Sorted Sets work, and what are their practical applications?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- List: ordered sequence — LPUSH/RPUSH add to ends; LPOP/RPOP remove from ends; LRANGE for slice
- List use cases: message queue (BLPOP for blocking pop), activity feed, recent items
- Set: unordered, unique values — SADD, SMEMBERS, SISMEMBER, SUNION, SINTER, SDIFF
- Set use cases: unique visitors per day, user interests, tags
- Sorted Set (ZSet): unique values with a float score — ranking, leaderboard, range queries
- ZADD, ZRANK, ZRANGE, ZRANGEBYSCORE, ZINCRBY — sorted set operations
- Sorted set use cases: leaderboards, rate limiting by timestamp, priority queues

sections.Title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Redis Lists are doubly-linked lists — you can push and pop from either end. The BLPOP command makes them work as a simple message queue — consumers block waiting for messages and get them immediately when they arrive. This is useful for simple task queues without the complexity of a full message broker.

Sets store unique values. The interesting operations are set mathematics — union, intersection, difference. You can find users who visited pages A and B (intersection), users who visited either page (union), or users who visited A but not B (difference). These are instant operations regardless of set size.

Sorted Sets are one of Redis's most powerful data structures. Every member has an associated floating-point score and members are kept sorted by score. This makes them perfect for leaderboards — ZADD to add/update a score, ZREVRANK to get someone's rank, ZREVRANGE to get the top N players. The score can also be a timestamp, enabling time-windowed operations like getting all events in the last hour.

questions.title: Distributed Locking with Redis
questions.question: How do you implement a distributed lock with Redis and what are the edge cases to handle?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Distributed lock: ensures only one instance in a cluster executes a critical section
- SET key value NX PX ttl: atomic set-if-not-exists with expiry — prevents deadlocks
- Lock value must be unique per holder (UUID) — prevents releasing someone else's lock
- Release: check value before delete (Lua script) — atomic check-and-delete
- Redlock algorithm: acquire lock on majority of N Redis nodes for stronger guarantees
- Redisson: battle-tested distributed lock implementation for Java
- Edge cases: lock expiry during long operation (lock renewal), network partition, Redis failover

sections.Title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A distributed lock ensures that a critical section executes on only one application instance at a time across a cluster. Redis is a popular choice because the SET key value NX PX command atomically sets a key only if it doesn't exist, with an expiry. The expiry prevents a lock from being held forever if the lock holder crashes.

The lock value must be a unique identifier per holder — typically a UUID. This prevents a subtle bug where instance A holds a lock, the lock expires due to slowness, instance B acquires the lock, and then instance A tries to release it — and incorrectly releases B's lock. By checking that the value matches before deleting, you ensure you only release your own lock.

The check-and-delete must be atomic. Reading and deleting separately has a race condition: instance A reads and confirms the value matches, instance B's lock expires in between, and then A deletes B's new lock. The solution is a Lua script, which Redis executes atomically.

questions.title: Redis Caching Patterns
questions.question: What are the main Redis caching patterns — cache-aside, write-through, and how do you handle cache invalidation?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Cache-aside (lazy loading): app checks cache first, loads from DB on miss, populates cache
- Write-through: write to cache and DB simultaneously — cache always current, more write latency
- Write-behind (write-back): write to cache, async write to DB — fast writes, risk of data loss
- Cache invalidation: delete on update/delete — simplest and safest strategy
- Cache stampede (thundering herd): many cache misses simultaneously overwhelming DB
- Stampede prevention: probabilistic early expiration, mutex/lock on cache miss
- Spring Cache abstraction: @Cacheable, @CacheEvict, @CachePut — declarative caching

sections.Title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Cache-aside, also called lazy loading, is the most common pattern. The application checks the cache first. On a hit, it returns the cached value. On a miss, it fetches from the database, stores the result in the cache, and returns it. The cache only contains data that has actually been requested, so you don't waste memory caching data nobody needs.

The invalidation strategy for cache-aside is eviction on update — when you update or delete data, you delete the corresponding cache key. The next request will be a miss and repopulate from the database. This is simple and correct, though it means the first request after an invalidation always hits the database.

The cache stampede problem happens when a popular cache entry expires and many concurrent requests all find a cache miss and simultaneously query the database. The solution is either to set a soft TTL and refresh proactively before expiry, or to use a distributed lock so only one request queries the database and the others wait for the cache to be populated.

questions.title: Redis Streams for Event Processing
questions.question: What are Redis Streams and how do they compare to Kafka for event processing?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Redis Streams: append-only log — like Kafka but within Redis
- XADD: append entry with auto-generated ID (timestamp-sequence)
- XREAD: read entries; XREADGROUP: consumer group with acknowledgment
- Consumer groups: multiple consumers, each message delivered to one consumer, track ACK
- Persistent: stream survives Redis restart (if persistence enabled)
- MAXLEN: cap stream size to prevent unbounded growth
- vs Kafka: Redis Streams simpler, no partition concept, fewer durability guarantees
- Use case: lightweight event bus, activity feeds, small-scale event sourcing
- Spring Data Redis: StreamOperations + @StreamListener (Spring Integration)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Redis Streams is an append-only data structure — like a Kafka topic but built into Redis. Producers append messages with XADD, each getting a timestamp-based ID. Consumers read messages with XREAD, optionally using consumer groups to distribute processing across multiple consumers while guaranteeing each message goes to exactly one consumer in the group.

The practical use case for Redis Streams is when you already have Redis in your stack and need lightweight event messaging without adding Kafka's operational complexity. For simple event broadcasting — like activity feeds, audit logs, or notification queues — Redis Streams is a great fit. For high-throughput, mission-critical event streaming with strong durability guarantees, use Kafka.

The key limitation compared to Kafka is durability. Redis is primarily an in-memory store — even with persistence, there's a window where unflused data can be lost. Kafka uses disk-based replication with very strong durability guarantees. For financial transactions or any data you absolutely cannot lose, Kafka is the right choice.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Redis Streams CLI

```bash
# XADD: append entry to stream, auto-generate ID
XADD user-events * action login userId 42 ip 1.2.3.4
# Returns: 1700000000000-0  (timestamp-sequence ID)

# XADD with max length (prevent unbounded growth)
XADD user-events MAXLEN ~ 10000 * action login userId 42
# ~ = approximate trimming (more efficient than exact)

# XREAD: read from stream
XREAD COUNT 10 STREAMS user-events 0  # from beginning
XREAD COUNT 10 STREAMS user-events $  # only new entries
XREAD BLOCK 5000 COUNT 10 STREAMS user-events $  # block 5s for new entries

# XRANGE: read range by ID
XRANGE user-events - +           # all entries
XRANGE user-events 1700000000000-0 +  # from specific entry
XRANGE user-events - + COUNT 10  # first 10 entries
```

## Consumer Groups

```bash
# Create consumer group (start from beginning: 0; or from now: $)
XGROUP CREATE user-events analytics-group 0 MKSTREAM

# Consumer reads (exclusive — not delivered to other consumers)
XREADGROUP GROUP analytics-group consumer-1 COUNT 10 STREAMS user-events >
# > = only undelivered messages

# Acknowledge processed message
XACK user-events analytics-group 1700000000000-0

# Check pending (delivered but not acked — need retry?)
XPENDING user-events analytics-group - + 10
```

## Spring Data Redis Streams

```java
@Service
public class UserEventProducer {
    private final StreamOperations<String, String, String> streamOps;

    public void publishLoginEvent(Long userId, String ip) {
        Map<String, String> event = Map.of(
            "action", "login",
            "userId", userId.toString(),
            "ip", ip,
            "timestamp", Instant.now().toString()
        );
        streamOps.add(StreamRecords.newRecord()
            .in("user-events")
            .ofMap(event));
    }
}

@Component
public class UserEventConsumer implements StreamListener<String, MapRecord<String, String, String>> {

    @Override
    public void onMessage(MapRecord<String, String, String> record) {
        Map<String, String> body = record.getValue();
        String action = body.get("action");
        String userId = body.get("userId");
        log.info("User {} performed action: {}", userId, action);
        // Redis auto-acks if using @EnableRedisStreams listener container
    }
}
```

## Redis Streams vs Kafka

```
                    Redis Streams    Kafka
Durability           Good (if AOF)   Excellent (disk replicated)
Throughput           High            Very High
Partitioning         No              Yes (horizontal scale)
Schema enforcement   No              Yes (Schema Registry)
Message retention    MAXLEN cap      Configurable (days/TB)
Setup complexity     Zero (already Redis)  Moderate
Best for             Lightweight     Mission-critical
                     event bus       event streaming
```

speakable_v2.hook: Redis Streams is an append-only data structure — like a Kafka topic but built into Redis.
speakable_v2.cap: For financial transactions or any data you absolutely cannot lose, Kafka is the right choice.
